The gerrymander is the rare political artifact that is both a crime scene and a folk tale. Every decade, after the census, legislatures sit down with maps and decide which neighbors will share a representative. The stated aim is equal population. The actual aim, in too many chambers, is to waste the other party's votes. Pack them into one lopsided district, or crack them across several, until a statewide minority can still hold a statewide majority. The practice is older than the word. The word is older than the outrage that now accompanies it.

Critics call the latest round a Hail Mary pass by a party that can feel the demographics shifting under its feet. That metaphor is doing a lot of work. A Hail Mary is a desperate throw at the buzzer, visible, theatrical, and usually incomplete. A durable gerrymander is the opposite: quiet, legalistic, and designed to survive the news cycle. It hides in committee rooms and in the fine print of precinct splits. By the time the public notices, the ball is already in the end zone.

Courts have tried to draw a line between politics and math. The line does not hold. Politics is how the math gets chosen. A compactness score can be gamed; a "community of interest" can be defined after the fact to bless a salamander-shaped district that happens to protect an incumbent. The Voting Rights Act still constrains the worst racial gerrymanders in some states, but partisan gerrymanders have spent a decade in a doctrinal fog. The Supreme Court has called them non-justiciable in federal court, which is a polite way of saying: take it up with the people who drew the maps.

That advice would be funny if it were not the entire trick. The people who drew the maps are the people you would have to elect by crossing the maps. It is a lock with the key inside. Independent commissions are the usual reform, and they help when they are real. Too often they are theater with a staff attorney who used to work for the majority leader. Transparency is not the same as power.

There is a temptation, especially among people who like dashboards, to treat this as a data problem that better algorithms will solve. Algorithms can detect outliers. They cannot confer legitimacy. A perfectly compact map can still disenfranchise a city. A messy map can still be the only way to keep a community whole. The question is not whether a machine can draw a prettier shape. The question is who is allowed to decide what "fair" means, and whether that decision can be reversed without a constitutional convention.

Take the latest maps with a grain of salt, then. The press conferences will talk about communities and continuity. The shapefiles will talk about vote share. Follow the shapefiles. And remember that a republic that cannot throw out a rigged referee will eventually stop showing up to the game. That is not a metaphor from football. It is a description of turnout.

Federalism complicates the morality play. Some states have already taken the maps away from the legislature. Others have doubled down, daring the Department of Justice to spend political capital it may not have. The census itself is a battlefield: undercounts in cities, overcounts in snowbird counties, a citizenship question that came and went like a storm cloud. If the raw headcount is contested, every subsequent line on the map inherits the argument.

Reformers talk about ranked-choice voting and multi-member districts as if changing the scoring system will discipline the players. Sometimes it does. More often the players hire new consultants. The incentive is durable because the prize is durable: a decade of safe seats, a decade of committee gavels, a decade in which primary voters matter more than general-election ones. Polarization is not only a mood. It is an equilibrium produced by the maps.

None of this requires a conspiracy. It requires a calendar, a lawyer, and a party that can count. The public's attention is seasonal. Redistricting is not. That asymmetry is the whole game, and it will still be the game the next time the census vans go out.
